clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Supportive management: sodium and fluid restriction, loop diuretics (Furosemide) for volume overload/edema, antihypertensives (calcium channel blocker or ACE inhibitor) for blood pressure control, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dark cola-colored urine, facial swelling, and high blood pressure after a sore throat

Key HPI features: 22F reports sudden appearance of dark, cola/tea-colored urine this morning along with puffiness around both eyes and mild headache. She had a severe untreated sore throat with fever approximately 2 weeks ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 156/98 (newly elevated), HR 78. Periorbital edema, 1+ pedal edema. Urinalysis: 3+ protein, 3+ blood, red blood cell (RBC) casts present under microscopy. Bloods: BUN 28, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, C3 complement level markedly low (34 mg/dL), C4 normal, Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer elevated.
Relevant background/PMH: Resolved pharyngitis 2 weeks ago
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to IgA nephropathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypertension or significantly reduced urine output — suggests more aggressive glomerular injury.
management_principles: Supportive management: sodium and fluid restriction, loop diuretics (Furosemide) for volume overload/edema, antihypertensives (calcium channel blocker or ACE inhibitor) for blood pressure control
Treat residual streptococcal colonization with oral Penicillin V if cultures positive
Monitor complement C3 levels for recovery over 6-8 weeks
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 22F presenting with acute nephritic syndrome (macrohematuria, periorbital edema, hypertension) 2 weeks post-streptococcal pharyngitis.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 156/98 (newly elevated), HR 78. Periorbital edema, 1+ pedal edema. Urinalysis: 3+ protein, 3+ blood, red blood cell (RBC) casts present under microscopy. Bloods: BUN 28, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, C3 complement level markedly low (34 mg/dL), C4 normal, Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer elevated.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) / Acute Nephritic Syndrome.
reference_soap.plan: Supportive management: sodium and fluid restriction, loop diuretics (Furosemide) for volume overload/edema, antihypertensives (calcium channel blocker or ACE inhibitor) for blood pressure control. Treat residual streptococcal colonization with oral Penicillin V if cultures positive. Monitor complement C3 levels for recovery over 6-8 weeks.

learning_objectives: Recognize classic triad of acute nephritic syndrome (hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension, edema)
Correlate latency period (1-3 weeks post-pharyngitis) and hypocomplementemia (low C3) with PSGN
Differentiate nephritic presentation from nephrotic presentation based on urinalysis and clinical signs
Formulate supportive management focusing on fluid restriction and blood pressure control

teaching.one_liner: An immune-complex reaction 1-3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection causes acute nephritic syndrome — cola-colored urine, facial swelling, and high blood pressure — from inflammation of the glomeruli, not a bladder infection.
red_flags: Severe hypertension or significantly reduced urine output — suggests more aggressive glomerular injury

must_ask.say: Did you have a bad sore throat or fever a couple of weeks ago?
What color is your urine — dark like cola or tea?
Is the swelling around your eyes worse in the morning?
Have you had a headache or felt your blood pressure might be high?
Has the amount of urine you're passing changed?
